source.title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems

accepted.question_text: Let k be a field, let X be an affine scheme over k with coordinate algebra A, and let a be a finite-dimensional k-algebra. Suppose an algebraic group Γ, rather than only a finite group, acts completely reducibly on both A and a by automorphisms. For the equivariant map algebra M(X,a)^Γ, defined as the fixed-point algebra (a ⊗ A)^Γ for the diagonal Γ-action, classify its irreducible finite-dimensional representations.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(a) More general groups Γ. Instead of a finite group Γ, one can consider, for instance, an algebraic group acting completely reducibly on A and a. The first step in the study of the resulting EMAs would be to classify their irreducible finite- dimensional representations.

accepted.question_text: Let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, let Γ act on X and on a target algebra by automorphisms, and define the corresponding equivariant map algebra as the Γ-fixed subalgebra of target ⊗ A. Develop the representation theory of such equivariant map algebras when the target algebra is much more general than the finite-dimensional Lie or associative cases, including infinite-dimensional Lie targets such as Kac-Moody or Heisenberg algebras and non-Lie targets such as alternative or Jordan algebras. In cases where finite-dimensional representations are defined, describe those representations.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(b) More general targets. There are many possible choices for the “target” alge- bra g for which the resulting EMA has not been studied. Even in the setting of Lie algebras, one could consider g to be, for instance, a Kac-Moody algebra (see [ERF] for the untwisted multiloop case) or some other well-studied infinite-dimensional Lie algebra, such as the Heisenberg algebra.

In fact, one can study the representation theory of any EMA for which the target is an algebra with well-defined representations. For example, it would be natural to consider the finite-dimensional representations in the case of alternative algebras or Jordan algebras.

accepted.question_text: Let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A and let Γ act compatibly on X and on a Lie superalgebra target, so that an equivariant map superalgebra is obtained by taking Γ-fixed equivariant maps. Generalize this setting by allowing the target to be any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra, replacing the commutative coordinate algebra A by a supercommutative algebra so that X is a superscheme, and replacing Γ by a Z2-graded group. Determine the resulting representation theory in this broader equivariant map superalgebra setting.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(c) Superschemes and superalgebras. The equivariant map superalgebra setting of [Sav] can be naturally generalized. First, one can consider more general Lie superalgebras for the target g. For example, one could take any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra (not just basic classical ones). Furthermore, one can replace A by a supercommutative algebra (in other words, let X be a superscheme) and Γ by a Z2 -graded group.

accepted.question_text: Replace the algebraic framework of equivariant map algebras with an analytic one. For a Banach manifold X, a Banach algebra a, and a group Γ acting by automorphisms, develop the theory and representation theory of algebras of Γ-equivariant differentiable maps from X to a.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(d) Analytic setting. Another interesting problem is to replace the algebraic setting by an analytic one. For example, let X be a Banach manifold, a a Banach algebra and consider equivariant differentiable maps X → a.

accepted.question_text: For equivariant map algebras M(X,a)^Γ, where X is an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, a is an algebra, Γ acts on X and a by automorphisms, and M(X,a)^Γ is the Γ-fixed subalgebra of a ⊗ A, determine classification criteria and invariants for the isomorphism problem. In particular, extend the known loop-algebra and two-variable multiloop-algebra results to the full multiloop case and then to more general equivariant map algebras.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.
4.2.1. Isomorphism problem. Characterizing EMAs up to isomorphism is one of the fundamental problems in the theory of EMAs.
It is therefore natural, though likely difficult, to try to generalize the results of both papers [ABP] and [GP07] to the multiloop case and beyond that to more general EMAs.

accepted.question_text: For equivariant map algebras M(X,a)^Γ, where M(X,a)^Γ is the Γ-fixed subalgebra of a ⊗ A for compatible actions on X and a, determine their automorphism groups in general. Extend the partial descriptions known in special untwisted, twisted-loop, multiloop, Lie-algebra, and Lie-superalgebra cases.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.
4.2.2. Automorphisms. Related to the problem of characterizing EMAs up to isomorphism, is the question of determining the automorphism groups of EMAs.

accepted.question_text: Let a be a finite-dimensional associative algebra over an algebraically closed field, let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, let Γ act on X and a by automorphisms, and set M = M(X,a)^Γ, the Γ-fixed subalgebra of a ⊗ A. Go beyond the classification of irreducible finite-dimensional M-modules by describing all indecomposable finite-dimensional M-modules and the block decomposition of the corresponding finite-dimensional module category.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

4.2.3. Indecomposable modules. The classification of the irreducible objects in the category of finite-dimensional modules of M for an associative a in Theorem 2.1 is only a first step towards a complete understanding of the category. Ideally, one would like to describe all of the indecomposable finite-dimensional modules and understand the block decomposition of this category.

accepted.question_text: Let a be an associative bialgebra, let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, let Γ act on X and a by automorphisms, and set M = M(X,a)^Γ, the Γ-fixed subalgebra of a ⊗ A. Understand the multi-orbit evaluation representations that arise from the comultiplication on a, including their construction, classification, and structural properties.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

4.2.4. Associative bialgebras. In the case that a is an associative bialgebra, one can naturally define multi-orbit evaluation representations using the comultiplica- tion on a. It would be interesting to understand these representations.

accepted.question_text: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let X be an affine scheme over k, let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k, let Γ act on X and g by automorphisms, and set M = M(X,g)^Γ, the Γ-fixed equivariant map Lie algebra. Compute the higher Ext groups between finite-dimensional M-modules, explain how these Ext groups interact with both the representation theory of g and the geometry of X, and determine how the global dimension of the finite-dimensional M-module category is governed by that geometry.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(a) Higher extensions. Only the first Ext groups are calculated in [NS], where it is shown that these groups are related to both the representation theory of the target g and the geometry of the scheme X (see, for instance, Proposition 3.5, which involves the tangent space). It is natural to try to compute higher Ext groups. One would expect a rich interplay between these groups and the geometry of the scheme X. It would be particularly interesting to see how the global dimension of the category of finite-dimensional modules is related to this geometry.

accepted.question_text: Let M be an equivariant map algebra M(X,g)^Γ, formed from an affine scheme X, a target algebra g, and a compatible Γ-action. Extend the theory of global and local Weyl modules from the currently understood cases to more general equivariant map algebras. This includes determining lengths, dimensions, and characters of local Weyl modules, and extending BGG reciprocity to this broader equivariant map algebra setting.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(b) Weyl modules. The study of (global and local) Weyl modules for EMAs is an active area of research. In particular, one would like to extend the results on the lengths, dimensions and characters of the local Weyl modules (see [CP01, BN04, CL06, CM04, FL07, Nak01, Nao12]) to the setting of more arbitrary EMAs (see [FMSa] for the definitions of global and local Weyl modules in this setting). It is also natural to try to extend the notion of BGG reciprocity described in [BCM12, BBC+ ] to a more general EMA setting (see [BBC+ , Rem. 2.7]).

accepted.question_text: Let M be an equivariant map algebra M(X,g)^Γ, formed from an affine scheme X, a target algebra g, and a compatible Γ-action. Develop representation-theoretic categories beyond finite-dimensional M-modules, including analogues of category O, categories of integrable highest-weight representations, categories of quasifinite representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces, and other suitable infinite-dimensional module categories.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

(c) Possibly infinite-dimensional representations. Much of the current focus in the study of the representation theory of arbitrary EMAs has been on the category of finite-dimensional representations. However, in specific cases (most importantly, the loop and current algebras) more general categories of representations have been studied.

It would be interesting to study analogous categories in the more arbitrary EMA setting. For example, one could consider the category of integrable highest weight rep- resentations, the category of quasifinite representations (i.e. representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces) or appropriate generalizations of category O.

accepted.question_text: Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let X be an affine scheme over k, let g be a semisimple finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k, let Γ act on X and g by automorphisms, and set M = M(X,g)^Γ. Describe the first cohomology group H1(M,V) for a general M-module V, extending the partial results known for some equivariant map algebras and locally finite modules. In particular, describe H1(M,Mad) for the adjoint M-module, equivalently the derivations of M modulo inner derivations.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

4.3.2. Cohomology. Assume g is semisimple. The formulas for ExtM (V1 , V2 ) proven in [NS] have a cohomological interpretation since ExtM (V1 , V2 ) ≃ H1(M, Homk(V1 , V2)). One can therefore expect that it should be possible to describe the first cohomol- ogy group H1 (M, V ) for a general M-module V . For some equivariant map alge- bras M, including multiloop algebras, and locally-finite M-modules, this is done in [NP]. A particular instance of this question is the adjoint module Mad , for which H1 (M, Mad ) = Derk (M)/ IDer(M).

accepted.question_text: Let M = M(X,g)^Γ be an equivariant map Lie algebra, formed from an affine scheme X, a Lie algebra g, and a compatible Γ-action, and let V be an M-module. Determine the homology groups H∗(M,V), including the structural consequences for the abelianization H0(M,Mad) = M / [M,M] of the adjoint module and for identifying perfect equivariant map algebras.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

A related problem is to determine the homology groups H∗ (M, V ). Some re- sults on H0 (M, Mad ) = M/[M, M] are contained in [NSS12] and [NS], see for example Lemmas 6.1 and 6.10 of [NS] describing classes of perfect equivariant map

algebras. The interest in perfect equivariant map algebras comes from Theorem 3.2 which indicates that these algebras have a simpler representation theory. A second reason is that perfect Lie algebras have universal central extensions, as discussed in Section 4.3.3 below.

accepted.question_text: Let M = (g ⊗ A)^Γ be a perfect equivariant map Lie algebra, formed from a Lie algebra g, a coordinate algebra A of an affine scheme X, and a compatible Γ-action. Understand the central extensions of M, especially its universal central extension uce(M). Determine when the universal central extension of the fixed-point algebra agrees with the fixed points of the universal central extension of the untwisted algebra, that is, when uce((g ⊗ A)^Γ) is naturally isomorphic to uce(g ⊗ A)^Γ.

evidence.quote: The action of Γ on X induces an action on the coordinate ring A of X. Then M = (a ⊗ A)Γ , the fixed points of the diagonal action of Γ on a ⊗ A.

4.3.3. Central extensions. Central extensions of Lie algebras often have a sim- pler representation theory, the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebras being a case in point. It is therefore of interest to understand central extensions of equivariant map alge- bras M, preferably the universal central extension uce(M) of a perfect M.

Generalizing the example of twisted loop algebras, one would like to relate the universal central extension of a perfect equivariant map algebra (g ⊗ A)Γ to the well-understood universal central extension uce(g ⊗ A). Observe that the action of Γ on g ⊗ A uniquely lifts to an action on uce(g ⊗ A). The formula one is aiming for is then very natural: uce((g ⊗ A)Γ) ≃ uce(g ⊗ A)Γ.
